In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed Allah is Hearing, Seeing.﴾

It is narrated that Khawla bint Tha'laba, the wife of Aws ibn al-Samit, brother of Ubada ibn al-Samit, was seen by her husband while she was praying. She had a beautiful body, and the man had a touch of lamam (a slight affliction of desire). When she finished her prayer, he sought to be intimate with her, but she refused. He became angry, and since he had a certain levity, he declared her unlawful to himself (zihar). She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Aws married me when I was young and desirable. When my years advanced and my children increased, he made me like his mother. I have small children: if I join them to him, they will be lost, and if I join them to me, they will go hungry."

Then there are two narrations here. It is reported that he (peace be upon him) said to her: "I have no ruling concerning your matter." And it is reported that he (peace be upon him) said to her: "You have become unlawful to him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, he did not mention divorce; he is the father of my children and the most beloved of people to me." He said: "You have become unlawful to him." She said: "I complain to Allah of my poverty and my grief." Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have become unlawful to him," she cried out and complained to Allah. While she was in this state, the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed color, and this verse was revealed. Then he (peace be upon him) sent for her husband and said: "What led you to do what you did?" He said: "Satan." He said: "Is there any concession?" He said: "Yes," and he recited to him the four verses, and said to him: "Can you free a slave?" He said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Can you fast?" He said: "No, by Allah. Were it not that I eat once or twice a day, my sight would fail, and I would think I am dying." He said to him: "Can you feed sixty needy persons?" He said: "No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah, unless you help me with a charity from you." So he helped him with fifteen sa' (measures), and Aws brought out an equal amount from his own, and he gave it in charity to sixty needy persons.

Know that in this report there are several discussions:

The first: Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: The meaning of "and he had a touch of lamam" in this report is not madness or insanity, for if he had that, then when he declared zihar in that state nothing would have been binding on him. Rather, the meaning of lamam here is the inclination toward women and intense eagerness and longing for them.

The second discussion: Zihar was among the most severe divorces of the Jahiliyya, because in prohibition it is the strongest possible. If that ruling became established by the Shari'a, the verse abrogates it (naskh, abrogation); otherwise it would not count as abrogation, because abrogation only enters into the sacred laws and not into the customs of the Jahiliyya. However, what is reported of him (ﷺ) saying to her "You have become unlawful" or "I see you have only become unlawful" is like an indication that it was a legislated ruling. As for what is reported that he paused regarding the ruling, that does not indicate this.

The third discussion: This incident shows that whoever's hope in the creation has been cut off, and no one remains for him in his affair except the Creator, Allah will suffice him in that affair.

Let us return to the exegesis. As for His saying: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿qad﴾ means expectation (tawaqqu'), because the Messenger of Allah and the woman who pleaded were both expecting that Allah would hear her pleading and complaint and would reveal what relieves her.

The second issue: Hamza used to assimilate the dal into the sin in ﴿qad sami'a﴾ and similar instances. Know that Allah the Exalted relates two matters about this woman:

The first of them: the pleading, which is His saying ﴿she who pleads with you concerning her husband﴾, that is, she pleads with you concerning the affair of her husband. And that pleading was that whenever he (peace be upon him) said to her, "You have become unlawful to him," she would say: "By Allah, he did not mention divorce."

The second of them: her complaint to Allah, which is her saying: "I complain to Allah of my poverty and my grief," and her saying: "I have small children." Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and Allah hears your mutual dialogue﴾. The word "muhawara" means mutual return in speech, from "haara al-shay'u yahuru hawran," meaning it returned, and from it: "We seek refuge in Allah from hawr after kawr" (returning after advancing), and from it: "fa-ma ahara bi-kalima," meaning he did not answer with a word. Then He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is Hearing, Seeing﴾, meaning He hears the speech of whoever calls upon Him and sees whoever humbles himself before Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 58, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

The Most High said: ﴿Those of you who divorce their wives by zihar (a pre-Islamic declaration that a wife is like one's mother's back, which made her unlawful to the husband), who say of their wives that they are not their mothers.﴾ Know that His saying ﴿Those who make zihar﴾ contains two issues.

The first issue concerns the linguistic and legal discussions, so we say: in this verse there are two investigations.
The first: what is zihar?
The second: who is the one who makes zihar?
His saying ﴿of their wives﴾ contains an investigation: who are the wives who are subject to zihar?

As for the first investigation, what is zihar, it has two positions.

The first position, concerning the lexical meaning of this word, has two opinions.
One: it is an expression for a man saying to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," so it is derived from ẓahr (back).
The second, which is the view of the author of al-Nazm, is that it is not derived from ẓahr in the sense of the body part, because the back is not more appropriate to mention in this context than the other organs that are places of intercourse and pleasure. Rather, ẓahr here is derived from height (ʿulūw), as in His saying ﴿So they could not scale it﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:97), meaning they could not climb over it. Whoever rises above something has "ẓahara" it. From this the mount is called ẓahr, because its rider is above it. Likewise a man's wife is his ẓahr, because he rises above her by right of intercourse, even though this is not from the direction of the back. So it is as if a man's wife is a mount for him and a back for him. What confirms this meaning is that the Arabs say about divorce, "I dismounted from my wife," meaning I divorced her. In their saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" there is an ellipsis and an implied element, because its interpretation is: "Your back is upon me," meaning my possession of you and my rising over you is unlawful, just as my rising over my mother and possessing her is unlawful for me.

The second position concerns the expressions used with this meaning in the usage of the Law. The basic form of this matter is that one says, "You are to me like the back of my mother." Either both the word "back" and the word "mother" are mentioned, or the word "mother" is mentioned without "back," or "back" is mentioned without "mother," or neither is mentioned. These are four categories.

The first category: when both are mentioned. This is accepted by consensus. There is then no dispute about the connecting particles as long as the sentence is complete. So if he says, "You are to me like the back of my mother," or "You are from me like the back of my mother," all these connecting forms are valid. If he does not use a connecting particle and says, "You are like the back of my mother," it is said that this is explicit, and it is said that it is possible he meant that she is like his mother's back with respect to someone else's right. But this possibility is like if he said to his wife, "You are divorced," and then said, "I meant by that to report that she is divorced by so-and-so's authority."

The second category: when the mother is mentioned but the back is not. The detailed position of al-Shafi'i on this is that the organs are of two kinds: some are such that comparing the wife to them does not suggest honor, and some are such that comparing her to them does suggest honor. As for the first kind, it is like his saying, "You are to me like the foot of my mother," or "like the hand of my mother," or "like the stomach of my mother." Al-Shafi'i has two opinions on it: the new (jadīd) view is that zihar is established, and the old (qadīm) view is that it is not established. As for the organs whose comparison is a cause of honor, it is like his saying, "You are to me like the eye of my mother," or "the spirit of my mother." If he intends zihar, it is zihar; if he intends honor, it is not zihar, because his wording admits that. If he speaks without specifying, there is hesitation. This is the detailed position of al-Shafi'i. As for the position of Abu Hanifa, Abu Bakr al-Razi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: if he compares his wife to a part of the mother that is lawful for him to look at, it is not zihar. This is his saying, "You are to me like the hand of my mother, or her head." But if he compares her to a part of the mother that is unlawful for him to look at, it is zihar, such as if he says, "You are to me like the stomach of my mother, or her thigh." My closer view is the old position of al-Shafi'i, which is that zihar is not valid with any of these expressions. The evidence for this is that the lawfulness of the wife was established, and the freedom of the obligation from expiation was established, and the basic rule regarding what is established is that it remains as it was. Abandoning this rule was only in the case of "You are to me like the back of my mother," for a meaning absent in the other cases. That is because the phrase known in the pre-Islamic period was "You are to me like the back of my mother," and for this reason it was called zihar. So this expression, by means of custom, indicated prohibition, and this meaning was not found in the other expressions, so it is necessary to remain with the ruling of the original state.

The third category: when the back is mentioned but the mother is not. This indicates three levels.

The first level: the comparison is to those who are prohibited by lineage or by nursing. On this there are two opinions: the old view is that it is not zihar, and the new view is that it is zihar, which is the position of Abu Hanifa.

The second level: comparing her to a woman who is prohibited temporarily, such as if he says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of so-and-so woman," and he had divorced her. The position I prefer is that none of this is zihar, and its proof is what we mentioned in the previous issue. The argument of Abu Hanifa is that the Most High said ﴿Those who make zihar﴾, and the apparent meaning of this verse requires that zihar arises with every prohibited woman. So whoever restricts it to the mother has made a specification. (The answer): when the Most High said after it, ﴿They are not their mothers﴾ and ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them﴾, this shows that what is meant by zihar is by mentioning the mother. Also, the prohibition of the mother is more severe than the prohibition of the other unlawful women. So we say: the factor requiring the continuation of lawfulness remains in place as we have explained, and this distinguishing feature exists, so it is necessary that analogy is not permitted.

The fourth category: when neither the back nor the mother is mentioned, such as if he says, "You are to me like the stomach of my sister." By the analogy of what came before, it must be that this is not zihar.

The second investigation concerns the one who makes zihar, and it has two issues.

* * *

The first issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the rule is that whoever's divorce is valid, his zihar is valid. Accordingly, the zihar of a dhimmi (a non-Muslim subject under Muslim protection) is valid in his view. Abu Hanifa said it is not valid. Al-Shafi'i argued from the generality of the Most High's saying ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives﴾. As for analogy, it is from two aspects:

The first: the effect of zihar in prohibition, and the dhimmi is qualified for this, as evidenced by the validity of his divorce. Once this is established, it is necessary that this action from him is valid by analogy with all other actions.

The second: expiation was only obligatory upon the Muslim as a deterrent from this act, which is an objectionable and false statement. This meaning exists regarding the dhimmi, so it is necessary that it be valid.

The proponents of Abu Hanifa's view argued from this verse in two ways:

The first: Abu Bakr al-Razi argued from the Most High's saying ﴿Those of you who make zihar from their wives﴾, and this is an address to the believers, so it indicates that zihar is specific to the believers.

The second: among the requirements of valid zihar is the obligation of fasting upon the one who returns and is unable to free a slave, based on the Most High's saying ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives, then return to what they said﴾ up to His saying ﴿So whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for two consecutive months﴾ (Al-Mujadila 58:4). And imposing fasting upon the dhimmi is impossible, because if it were obligatory, it would be obligatory either with disbelief, which is invalid by consensus, or after faith, which is invalid because of his saying ﴿Islam erases what came before it.﴾

(The answer) to the first, from several aspects:
One: His saying ﴿of you﴾ is a direct address, so it includes all those present. Why do you say it is specific to the believers? Suppose we grant that it is specific to the believers; why do you say that the specification of the believers in the mention indicates that the status of others is different? Especially since it is from the position of this speaker that specification by mention does not indicate that the status of what is other than it is different. Suppose we grant that it does indicate this; yet the indication of the implied meaning (mafhūm) is weaker than the indication of the explicit statement (manṭūq). So relying on the generality of His saying ﴿Those who make zihar﴾ is better. Suppose we grant equal strength; yet the position of Abu Hanifa is that a general text which comes after a specific text abrogates the specific text. What we relied upon, namely His saying ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives﴾ (Al-Mujadila 58:3), is later in mention than His saying ﴿Those of you who make zihar﴾. The apparent meaning is that it was also later in revelation, because His saying ﴿Those of you who make zihar﴾ does not contain an explanation of the ruling of zihar, while His saying ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives﴾ contains an explanation of the ruling of zihar. And that the explained text is later in revelation than the general, unexplained text is better.

(The answer) to the second, from several aspects:
The first: among its requirements is also that whenever he is unable to fast, he is sufficed with feeding. So here, if inability is established, he must be sufficed with feeding; and if it is not established, the question is resolved.
The second: fasting is a substitute for freeing a slave, and the substitute is weaker than the original. Then a slave is unable to free a slave, yet his zihar is valid. So if the loss of the stronger of the two requirements does not necessitate prohibition while zihar is valid, then how can the loss of the weaker of the two requirements prevent the position that zihar is valid?
The third: al-Qadi Husayn, one of our companions, said: it is said, "If you want to be freed from the prohibition, then embrace Islam and fast." As for his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, "Islam erases what came before it," we say: it is general, while the obligation of expiation is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. Also, we do not impose fasting upon him; rather we say: if you want to remove the prohibition, then fast; otherwise, do not fast.

The second issue: al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Malik, may Allah have mercy on them, said: the zihar of a woman against her husband is not valid. This is when a woman says to her husband, "You are to me like the back of my mother." Al-Awza'i said it is an oath which she expiates. This is an error, because a man is not obligated by it to an expiation of oath, and this is the basic rule; so how is it obligatory upon the woman? Also, zihar causes prohibition by speech, and a woman does not possess that, as evidenced by the fact that she does not possess divorce.

* * *

The third issue: al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: if he says, "You are to me like the back of my mother today," the zihar ends with the passing of the day. Malik and Ibn Abi Layla said: he is a person who makes zihar forever. Our proof: the prohibition resulting from zihar is capable of being time-limited, otherwise it would not be dissolved by expiation. And when it is capable of being time-limited, then if he limits it, it must be measured according to that limitation, by analogy with the oath.

This is what concerns the issues related to His saying ﴿Those who make zihar﴾. As for His saying ﴿from their wives﴾, the rulings of the one subjected to zihar are connected to it. The scholars differed over whether zihar is valid regarding a slave woman (amah). Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said it is not valid. Malik and al-Awza'i said it is valid. The argument of al-Shafi'i: the lawfulness was established, and expiation was not obligatory, and the basic rule regarding what is established is that it continues. The verse does not cover this case, because His saying ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives﴾ includes free wives but not slave women. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿or their women﴾ (Al-Nur 24:31), and what is understood from it is free women; were it not so, His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ could not validly be joined to it, because a thing is not conjoined to itself. And the Most High said ﴿and the mothers of your wives﴾, so this applies to wives, not to those owned by right of possession.

Fifth issue: the word "minkum" (from among you) in His words, ﴿Those of you who make their wives unlawful to themselves by zihar﴾, is a rebuke of the Arabs and a condemnation of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of the Jahiliyyah specifically, not among the other nations. His, may He be exalted, words ﴿They are not their mothers﴾ contain two issues.

First issue: Asim, in the transmission of al-Mufaddal, read "ummahatuhum" (their mothers) in the nominative, while the rest read it in the accusative according to the form of the genitive. The reading in the nominative is the dialect of Tamim. Sibawayh said: it is the more analogical of the two options, because negation is like interrogation; just as interrogation does not change the sentence from what it was, so negation should not change the sentence from what it was. The reading in the accusative is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and taking the revelation in their dialect is more fitting; and upon it came His words, ﴿This is not a human being﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. Its basis in analogy is that "ma" (not) resembles "laysa" (is not) in two respects:
One of them: "ma" enters upon the subject and the predicate, just as "laysa" enters upon both of them.
The second: "ma" negates what is present, just as "laysa" negates what is present. When resemblance arises from two aspects, equality in all the other rulings becomes necessary, except what is specified by evidence, by analogy with the category of what does not take tanwin.

Second issue: There is an difficulty in the verse. Whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," has likened the wife to the mother without saying that she is a mother. So how is it fitting that it be said, as a refutation of his statement, ﴿They are not their mothers﴾, and how is it fitting that it be said, ﴿And indeed they utter an evil word and a falsehood﴾?

The answer: As for the lie, it arises because his statement, "You are to me like the back of my mother," either makes it an report or an act of creation. On the first assumption, it is a lie, because the wife is lawful while the mother is forbidden, and likening the lawful to the forbidden in the attribute of lawfulness and forbiddenness is a lie. And if we take it as an act of creation, that is also a lie, because its being a creation means that the Shari'ah made it a cause for the occurrence of the prohibition; since the Shari'ah did not intend this comparison, making it a creation for the establishing of this ruling would be a lie and falsehood. Some have said: He, may He be exalted, only described it as "an evil word and a falsehood" because the mother is forbidden with a perpetual prohibition, while the wife does not become forbidden to him by this statement with a perpetual prohibition; therefore it is certainly an evil word and a falsehood. This view is weak, because likening one thing to another does not necessitate that the resemblance between them be in every respect; so from likening the wife to the mother in prohibition it does not follow that she is likened to her in the prohibition being perpetual, since the general notion of prohibition is broader than the perpetual and the temporary prohibition.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 58, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them, and indeed they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood.﴾ As for the discussion of the explanation of the word "allati" (those who), it has already been covered in Surat al-Ahzab at His saying: ﴿nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar (zihar, the pre-Islamic practice of likening one's wife to one's mother) your mothers.﴾ Then, there are two questions regarding the verse. The first is that its apparent meaning requires that there is no mother except the one who gave birth, and this is problematic, because He said in another verse: ﴿and your sisters through nursing﴾ [An-Nisa: 23], and in another verse: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 6]. This question cannot be answered by saying that the meaning of the nursing woman being a mother and the Messenger's wives being mothers is the prohibition of marriage; for we say: by this path it has become clear that the absence of true motherhood does not necessarily entail the absence of prohibition. Thus, the absence of the wife being a mother does not necessarily entail the absence of prohibition. The apparent meaning of the verse gives the impression that He, exalted is He, argued from the absence of motherhood to the absence of prohibition, and in that case the question is directed at it.

(The answer): The intended meaning from the apparent wording of the verse is not what the questioner mentioned. Rather, the implied sense of the verse is as if it were said: The wife is not a mother such that the prohibition would arise because of motherhood, and the Law did not intend to make this term a cause for the occurrence of the prohibition such that the prohibition would arise. Therefore, the prohibition does not arise there at all. Thus their description of her as forbidden was a lie and a falsehood.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, either without repentance for whomever He wills, as He said: ﴿and forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾, or after repentance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who divorce by zihar from their wives and then wish to retract what they said - then [the penalty is] the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "fa-ʿalayhim tahriru raqabah" (then upon them is the freeing of a slave), and it did not mention "ʿalayhim" (upon them), because there is an indication of it in the sentence. If you wish, you may supply "fa-kaffaratuhum tahriru raqabah" (then their expiation is the freeing of a slave).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾, know that people have greatly differed in the explanation of this phrase. It is necessary first to state the views of the grammarians regarding this phrase, and second to state the views of the jurists of the Sharia. There are issues in this:

The first issue: Al-Farra' said: There is no difference in language between saying: "yaʿudūna li-mā qālū" (they return to what they said), "ilā mā qālū" (to what they said), and "fī mā qālū" (concerning what they said). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the word "ila" (to) and the letter "li" (for) are interchangeable, as in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah who guided us to this﴾ [Al-A'raf: 43], and He said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [As-Saffat: 23], and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah﴾ [Hud: 36], and He said: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it [to do so]﴾ [Az-Zalzalah: 5].

The second issue: The phrase "mā qālū" (what they said) in His saying: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾ has two possibilities:

One of them: that it refers to the word of zihar itself, and the meaning is that they return to that utterance.

The second: that the intended meaning of His saying "lima qālū" (what they said) is the thing said about, which is what they made forbidden to themselves by the utterance of zihar, treating the saying as if it were the thing said about. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and We will inherit what he says﴾, meaning, we will inherit what is said about him (i.e., his property). And the Messenger, upon him be peace, said: "The one who takes back his gift is like the dog that returns to its vomit," though he is actually returning to the thing given. And a man says: "O Allah, You are our hope," meaning, the One we hope in. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [Al-Hijr: 99], meaning, the thing that is certain. Accordingly, the meaning of His saying: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾ is that they return to the thing about which they uttered that saying. Then, if we interpret this phrase according to the first possibility, we say: The lexicographers said: it is permissible to say "ʿada li-mā faʿala" (he returned to what he did), meaning he did it again, and it is permissible to say "ʿada li-mā faʿala," meaning he annulled what he did. This is a reasonable statement, because whoever does something and then wishes for its like to be said, has without doubt returned to that same reality; and likewise whoever does something and then wishes to nullify it, has returned to it, since disposing of a thing by annulling it is not possible except by returning to it.

The third issue: It has become clear from what we have presented that His saying: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾ may mean that they return to it by annulling, lifting, and removing it, and it may mean that they return to producing its like once more. As for the first possibility, it is the one that most of the independent jurists adopted, and they differed about it in several ways:

The first: This is the view of al-Shafi'i, that the meaning of returning to what they said is refraining from divorce after zihar for a period of time in which he is able to divorce her. This is because, when he made zihar, he intended the prohibition; if he links that with divorce, he has completed what he began of establishing the prohibition, and there is no expiation upon him. But if he remains silent about divorce, that indicates he regrets what he initiated of prohibition, and then expiation becomes obligatory upon him. Abu Bakr al-Razi, in "Ahkam al-Qur'an," argued against the soundness of this view on two grounds:

The first: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾, and "thumma" (then) implies delay, whereas according to this view the one who made zihar would be returning immediately after the utterance without any delay, and that contradicts the implication of the verse.

The second: He likened her to the mother, and the mother is not forbidden to be kept (as a wife); therefore likening the wife to the mother does not require the prohibition of keeping the wife. So keeping the wife does not constitute a contradiction of his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother," and therefore the return should not be explained by this keeping.

The answer to the first: This objection also applies to the view of Abu Hanifa, for he defined returning as seeking permission for intercourse, so the one who made zihar could not return to her by this definition immediately after finishing uttering the word of zihar, so that a delay would occur; yet the community is unanimous that he has that right. Thus it is established that this difficulty applies to him as well. Furthermore, we say: as long as a period has not passed in which he could divorce her, he is not judged to be returning. Thus his becoming a returner is delayed from his becoming a zihar-maker by that amount of time, and that suffices for acting upon the implication of the word "thumma."

The answer to the second: The mother is forbidden to be kept in the manner of marriage and forbidden to be enjoyed; so His saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" does not show that the likening occurred regarding keeping her in the manner of marriage, or regarding enjoyment of her. Therefore it must be understood as covering all of it. So the saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" requires likening her to the mother in the prohibition of keeping her in the manner of marriage. If he does not divorce her, he has kept her in the manner of marriage, and this keeping contradicts the implication of his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother," so it is obligatory to judge him as a returner. This is a summarized statement of the position of al-Shafi'i.

The second view regarding the explanation of returning, which is the view of Abu Hanifa: it is an expression for seeking permission for intercourse, touching, and looking at her with desire. They said: This is because when he likened her to the mother in the prohibition of these things, and then intended to make these things permissible, that would contradict his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother." Know that this statement is weak, because when he likened her to the mother, he did not specify in which of these things he likened her to her. So directing this likening to the prohibition of enjoyment and the prohibition of looking is no more appropriate than directing it to the prohibition of keeping her in the manner of marriage. Therefore this likening must be understood as covering all of it. And since that is so, if he keeps her in the manner of marriage for a moment, he has annulled the ruling of his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother," so the return must be realized.

The third view regarding the explanation of returning, which is the view of Malik: that returning to her is an expression for resolving to have intercourse with her. This is weak, because the intention to have intercourse with her does not contradict her being forbidden; what contradicts her being forbidden is the intention to make intercourse with her permissible. Accordingly, we return to the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him.

The fourth view regarding the explanation of returning, which is the view of Tawus and al-Hasan al-Basri: that returning to her is an expression for having intercourse with her. This is an error, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then wish to retract what they said, then [the penalty is] the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾, with the particle of sequence "fa" in His saying "fa-tahriru raqabah" (then the freeing of a slave), requires that the expiation comes after the return, and His saying "min qabli an yatamassa" (before they touch one another) requires that the expiation comes before intercourse. Since it is established that the expiation must come after the return and before intercourse, it follows that the return is other than intercourse. Know that our companions (the Shafi'is) said: the return mentioned here, granting that it is suitable for intercourse, or for resolving to have intercourse, or for seeking permission for intercourse, yet what al-Shafi'i said, may Allah have mercy on him, is the least thing to which the term applies, so the ruling must be attached to it, because it is by it that the designation of return is realized; as for the rest, it is an addition for which there is absolutely no proof.

The second possibility: regarding His saying: ﴿then wish to retract﴾, i.e., they do the like of what they did. On this possibility too there are several views:

The first: Al-Thawri said: the return is the repetition of zihar in Islam. Its explanation: the people of the Jahiliyya used to divorce by zihar, so Allah, exalted is He, made the ruling of zihar in Islam different from their ruling in the Jahiliyya. He said: ﴿Those of you who make zihar from their wives﴾, meaning in the Jahiliyya, ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾, meaning in Islam; and the meaning is that they say in Islam the same as they used to say in the Jahiliyya, and then its expiation is such-and-such. Our companions said: this view is weak, because He mentioned zihar and mentioned the return after it with "thumma," and this requires that the return be something other than zihar. If they say: the meaning is "those who used to make zihar from their wives before Islam," and the Arabs omit the word "kana" (was), as in His saying: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 102], meaning what the devils used to recite. We reply: omission is contrary to the original usage.

The second view: Abu al-Aliyah said: if he repeats the word of zihar, then he has returned; if he does not repeat it, it is not a return. This is the view of the Zahiris, and they argued for it by saying that the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿then wish to retract what they said﴾ indicates repeating what they did, and this can only be by repetition. This too is weak on two grounds:

The first: If this were the intended meaning, He would have said: "thumma yu'idun ma qalu" (then they repeat what they said).

The second: The hadith of Aws, for he did not repeat the zihar; he only resolved to have intercourse, and the Messenger imposed the expiation upon him. Likewise the hadith of Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi, who said: "I could not refrain from intercourse, and when Ramadan came, I made zihar with my wife, fearing that I would not be able to refrain from her after the dawn; so I made zihar with her for the whole month of Ramadan, then I could not refrain, so I had intercourse with her. I came to the Messenger and informed him of that, and I said: Carry out upon me the judgment of Allah. He said: 'Free a slave.'" So the Messenger, upon him be peace, made the expiation obligatory, though he did not mention repetition of zihar.

The third view: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: the meaning of return is that he swears to what he first said of the word of zihar. For if he does not swear, expiation is not obligatory on him, by analogy with what if he said regarding some food: "It is forbidden to me like the flesh of a human," then expiation is not obligatory on him. But if he swears to it, the expiation of an oath becomes obligatory on him. This too is weak, because expiation is obligatory by consensus in the rites of pilgrimage where there is no oath, and in the case of accidental killing where there is no oath either.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then [the penalty is] the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾, there are issues concerning it:

* * *

The first issue: They differed about what zihar makes forbidden. Al-Shafi'i has two positions:

One of them: that it forbids only intercourse.

The second position, which is the more apparent: that it forbids all kinds of enjoyment. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and his evidence consists of several points:

(Part 2 of 2) Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 58, verse 3

The first (proof): His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then freeing a slave before they touch one another﴾. So this applies generally to all kinds of touching, whether by the hand or otherwise.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who make zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula, "you are to me as the back of my mother") from their wives﴾. He imposed the ruling of prohibition on him because he likened her to the back of his mother. Just as touching the back of one's mother and contact with it are prohibited to him, it is necessary that the situation regarding the wife be the same.

The third: 'Ikrimah narrated: "A man made zihar from his wife, then had intercourse with her before he had made expiation. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and he said: 'Keep away from her until you have made expiation.'"

**The second issue:** The scholars differed regarding one who makes zihar repeatedly. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: each zihar requires an expiation, unless it occurs in one session, in which case the repetition is taken as emphasis and he owes one expiation. Malik said: whoever makes zihar from his wife a hundred times in separate sessions owes only one expiation. Our evidence is that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who make zihar from their wives﴾ ﴿then freeing a slave﴾ requires that zihar be the cause (*'illah*) for the obligation of expiation. When a second zihar occurs, the cause of the obligation of expiation has occurred. The second zihar is either the cause of the first expiation or of a second expiation. The first is invalid, because the expiation became obligatory by the first zihar, and bringing into being what already exists is impossible; and because the delay of the cause after the ruling is impossible. Therefore we know that the second zihar requires a second expiation. Malik argued that His saying, "those who make zihar," includes the one who makes zihar once and the one who makes it many times, and then He obligated on him the freeing of a slave; so we know that one expiation is sufficient for zihar, whether it occurred once or many times.

The answer: He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you to account for what you have intentionally bound by oaths; its expiation is the feeding of ten needy persons﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. This requires that for many oaths only one expiation is obligatory. Since that is invalid, so too is what you have asserted.

**The third issue:** A man has four wives under him, and he makes zihar from all of them with one statement, saying: "You are to me like the back of my mother." Al-Shafi'i has two opinions. The more apparent is that he is obliged to pay four expiations, in view of the number of those from whom he made zihar. Its evidence is what we mentioned: that he made zihar regarding this one, so an expiation became binding on him because of this zihar; and he also made zihar regarding that one, so the second zihar must necessarily require another expiation.

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that expiation is obligatory before touching. If he had intercourse before making expiation, only one expiation is obligatory on him. This is the view of most scholars, such as Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, Sufyan, Ahmad and Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on them. Some said: if he had intercourse with her before making expiation, he owes two expiations. This is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi. Our evidence is that the verse indicates that expiation is obligatory on the one who makes zihar before returning. Here the quality of being prior is lost, so the basic obligation of expiation remains. There is no indication in the verse that failing to do it first requires another expiation.

**The fifth issue:** The more apparent view is that it is not fitting for the wife to allow him to approach her until he has made expiation. If he is negligent about making expiation, the ruler (*imam*) comes between him and her and compels him to make expiation, and if necessary by beating, until he fulfils her right to intercourse. The jurists said: none of the expiations is enforced by compulsion or imprisonment except the expiation of zihar alone, because failing to make expiation is harm to the wife and refusal to fulfil her right.

**The sixth issue:** Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this slave is valid whether he is a believer or a disbeliever, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then freeing a slave﴾. This expression conveys generality over all slaves. Al-Shafi'i said: he must be a believer. His evidence is two-fold:

The first: The polytheist is impure, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and every impure thing is wicked by the consensus of the community; and He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not aim at the wicked﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267].

The second: We are agreed that the slave in the expiation for killing is restricted to being a believer. So likewise here, the common factor being that manumission is a favour. Restricting it to belief requires directing this favour to the friends of Allah and withholding it from the enemies of Allah. Not restricting it to belief may lead to depriving the friends of Allah; so it is necessary that it be restricted to belief in order to achieve this benefit.

**The seventh issue:** Manumitting a *mukatab* (a slave contracted to buy his freedom) is not valid according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if he manumits him before he has paid anything, it is valid for the expiation; if he manumits him after he has paid something, the apparent narration is that it is not valid. Al-Hasan narrated from Abu Hanifah that it is valid. Abu Hanifah's argument is that the *mukatab* is a slave (*raqabah*), because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and for the slaves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60], and a slave is valid, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then freeing a slave﴾. Al-Shafi'i's argument is that the factor requiring the continuation of the obligations through the manumission of a slave remains after the manumission of the *mukatab*, and what caused the cessation of acting on it in the case of slaves is not present here; so it is necessary that it remain on the original basis. The explanation of the factor: the basic principle concerning what is established is that it remains as it was. The explanation of the distinguishing point: the *mukatab* is like one who has departed from the ownership of his master, though he has not departed from his ownership, yet a deficiency can occur in his servitude; this is shown by the fact that he has become more entitled to his earnings, and the master is prohibited from disposing of him; and if the master destroys him, he must pay his value; and if he has intercourse with his *mukatabah* (female *mukatab*), he is fined the bridal payment. It is well known that removing pure ownership, free of any taint of weakness, is harder on the owner than removing weak ownership. Nor does it follow that a man's discharge of the obligation by manumitting an ordinary (*qinn*) slave means his discharge of the obligation by manumitting a *mukatab*.

The second point: We are agreed that if the heir manumits him after his death, it is not valid for the expiation. So likewise, if the deceased (the *muwarrith*) manumitted him; and the common factor is that the ownership is weak.

**The eighth issue:** If he buys a close relative who becomes free upon him (by law) with the intention of expiation, that relative is manumitted for him, but it does not count as an expiation according to al-Shafi'i. According to Abu Hanifah it does count. Abu Hanifah's argument is adherence to the apparent wording of the verse. Al-Shafi'i's argument is what has preceded.

**The ninth issue:** Abu Hanifah said: feeding in expiations is fulfilled by enabling (*tamkin*) the needy to have food. According to al-Shafi'i it is fulfilled only by transferring ownership (*tamlik*) to the poor person. Abu Hanifah's argument is the apparent Qur'an, which is that what is obligatory is feeding, and the true meaning of feeding is enabling; this is shown by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. That is fulfilled by enabling and by transferring ownership, so likewise here. Al-Shafi'i's argument is analogy with zakat and the charity of breaking the fast (*sadaqat al-fitr*).

**The tenth issue:** Al-Shafi'i said: for each needy person, one *mudd* of food from the food of his land on which he subsists, whether wheat, barley, rice, dates or dried curd (*aqit*); this is by the *mudd* of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a *mudd* that came into being after him is not taken into account. Abu Hanifah said: each needy person is to be given half a *sa'* of wheat, flour or roasted grain (*sawiq*), or a *sa'* of dates or a *sa'* of barley, and it does not suffice him to give less than that. Al-Shafi'i's argument is that the apparent wording of the verse requires feeding, and the degrees of feeding vary in quantity and quality; so there is no preference for taking the word as referring to some of them over taking it as referring to the rest. Therefore it must be taken to the least that is necessarily apparent, and that is the *mudd*. Abu Hanifah's argument is what has been related in the hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit: ("For each needy person, half a *sa'* of wheat"); and from 'Ali and 'A'ishah, who both said: "For each needy person, two *mudd* of wheat." Also, what is considered is the need of the day for each needy person, so it is analogous to the charity of breaking the fast, and that is not fulfilled by the *mudd* but by what we have said; so likewise here.

**The eleventh issue:** If he feeds one needy person sixty times, it is not valid according to al-Shafi'i, but according to Abu Hanifah it is valid. Al-Shafi'i's argument is the apparent wording of the verse, which is that He obligated the feeding of sixty needy persons; so it is necessary to observe the apparent wording of the verse. Abu Hanifah's argument is that the aim is to remove need, and that is achieved. Al-Shafi'i may respond: arbitrary determinations are prevalent in these estimations, so analogy must be refrained from in them. Also, perhaps bringing joy into the heart of sixty people is closer to the pleasure of Allah, Exalted is He, than bringing joy into the heart of one person.

**The twelfth issue:** The followers of al-Shafi'i said: He, Exalted is He, said regarding the slave: ﴿But whoever does not find [the means], then fasting for two months﴾, and He said regarding fasting: ﴿But whoever is not able, then feeding sixty needy persons﴾. So in the first He said: ﴿whoever does not find﴾, and in the second: ﴿whoever is not able﴾. They said: one whose wealth is absent does not transfer to fasting because of his inability to manumit at the present time. As for one who is ill at present, he transfers to feeding, even if his illness is such that its removal is hoped for. They said: the difference is that in the transfer to feeding He said: ﴿whoever is not able﴾, and one who is not able because of present illness and immediate incapacity is not able. Regarding the slave He said: ﴿whoever does not find﴾, and the meaning is whoever does not find a slave or the wealth with which to buy a slave; and one whose wealth is absent is not called one who lacks wealth. Also it may be said in the difference: bringing wealth depends on one's choice, whereas removing illness is not within one's choice.

**The thirteenth issue:** Some of our companions said: excessive sexual desire and raging lust is an excuse for transferring to feeding. The evidence for this is that when he (peace be upon him) ordered the Bedouin to fast, the man said to him: "Was I not overcome only because of fasting?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Feed." The hadith indicates that intense sexual desire is an excuse for transferring from fasting to feeding. Also, *istita'ah* (ability) is beyond *wus'* (capacity), and *wus'* is beyond *taqah* (power). *Istita'ah* is that a person be able to do the act with ease; and it is well known that this meaning is not complete with intense sexual desire. This is a brief summary of what relates to the jurisprudence of the Qur'an in this verse, and Allah knows best.

* His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "That" refers to the severity of the expiation, ﴿you are admonished with﴾, meaning that the severity of the expiation is an admonition to you so that you abandon zihar and do not return to it. Others said: ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾, meaning you are commanded by it, the expiation; ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, of making expiation and of abandoning it.

Then He, Exalted is He, mentioned the ruling for one who is unable to find a slave, saying: ﴿So whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months before they touch one another. And whoever is not able, then feeding sixty needy persons﴾. The verse indicates that consecutiveness is a condition. He mentioned that freeing the slave and fasting must both occur before touching; then He mentioned that whoever is not able to do that must feed sixty needy persons, and He did not mention that it must occur before touching; yet it is like the first two by the indication of consensus. The derivative jurisprudential issues that branch from this verse are numerous and are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger. These are the limits of God. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ In His words ﴿That﴾ there are two possibilities:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: it is in the place of the nominative (raf'), and the meaning is: "The obligation is that which We have set down."

The second: We made that clarification and instruction of the rulings so that you would affirm belief in God and His Messenger by acting upon their laws, and so that you would not persist in the rulings of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance), such as making zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce by likening one's wife to one's mother) the strongest type of divorce. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah used the lam in His words ﴿so that you may believe﴾ as evidence that God's act is causally motivated by a purpose, and that His purpose is that you believe in God and not persist in what you were upon of disbelief in the Jahiliyya. This indicates that He, exalted is He, wanted from them belief and the absence of disbelief.

The second issue: Whoever includes action within the definition of faith (iman) uses this verse as evidence, saying: He commanded them with these deeds and clarified that He commanded them with them so that by performing them they would become believers; so the verse indicates that action is part of faith. Whoever denies this says: He, exalted is He, did not say ﴿that you may believe in God﴾ by performing these things. We say: the meaning is: "That you may believe in God by affirming these rulings." Then He, exalted is He, emphasized, in explaining that obedience is necessary for them, ﴿These are the limits of God. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾, meaning: for whoever denies this and rejects it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 58, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated just as those before them were humiliated, and We have certainly sent down clear signs. And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾

In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Concerning al-muhaddah (opposition, hostility), there are two opinions. Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of al-muhaddah is al-mumana'ah (preventing, restraining), and from it the doorkeeper is called haddad (one who keeps out), and the one who is denied provision is called mahdud (restricted).

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: al-muhaddah is a form of mufa'alah derived from the word al-hadid (iron), and the meaning is confrontation with iron, whether that is literally so or is an intense dispute resembling a quarrel with iron. As for the exegetes, they said: yuhaddduna means yu'adduna (they oppose) and yushaqqqna (they oppose and contend with), and this occurs at times by warring against the friends of Allah, and at times by denying and barring from the religion of Allah.

The second issue: The pronoun in His saying ﴿yuhaddduna﴾ may refer to the hypocrites, for they used to show affection to the disbelievers and back them against the Messenger, peace be upon him, so Allah humiliated them, and it may include the rest of the disbelievers. Allah informed His Messenger that they ﴿kubitu﴾, i.e., were forsaken. Al-Mubarrad said: it is said, "Kabata Allahu fulanan" when Allah humiliates someone, and the one who is repelled in humiliation is called maknub. Then He said: ﴿just as those before them were humiliated﴾ from among the enemies of the messengers, ﴿and We have certainly sent down clear signs﴾ which indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger; ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾ with these signs ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾ which takes away their might and arrogance. Thus He, glorified is He, made clear that the punishment of these opponents in this world is humiliation and disgrace, and in the Hereafter is severe punishment.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that by which this threat is completed, and said:

"Yawma" is in the accusative, governed either by "yunabbi'uhum" (He will inform them) or by "muhin" (humiliating), or by an implied "udhkur" (remember), to magnify the Day. Regarding His words "jami'an" (all together) there are two opinions:

The first: all of them, none of them is left unraised.

The second: gathered together in one state. Then He said: "then He will inform them of what they did," as a means of shaming them, rebuking them, and exposing their condition, in which they wish to be hurried to the Fire because of the disgrace that will befall them before all witnesses.

As for His words: "Allah has enumerated it" (ahsahu Allah), meaning He has encompassed all the circumstances of those deeds, in respect of quantity, quality, time and place, because He, exalted is He, has knowledge of the particulars. Then He said: "and they forgot it" (wa nasuhu), because they considered them insignificant and treated them lightly; so, inevitably, they forgot them. "And Allah is Witness over everything" (wa Allahu 'ala kulli shay'in shahid), meaning He is ever-present, nothing whatsoever being hidden from Him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Have you not seen" means, "Have you not known?" I say: this is true, because His being All-Knowing of things is not seen, but He is known through proofs. The word "seeing" (ruʾya) was applied to this knowledge because the proof of His being All-Knowing is that His acts are firm, perfected, coherent and orderly, and whoever's acts are like this is knowing.

As for the first premise: it is perceptible and observed in the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and in the compositions of plants and animals.

As for the second premise: it is self-evident. Since the proof indicating that He, exalted is He, is such is manifest, this knowledge and the reasoning reach the highest degrees of clarity and evidentness, so it becomes as though it were perceived by the senses and observed. Therefore He applied the word "seeing" and said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. As for His, exalted is He, being Knowing of all things known, that is because His knowledge is eternal knowledge. So if it related to some things and not others, given that all knowables are shared in the validity of being knowable, that knowledge would require a specifier in that specification, and that is impossible for God, exalted is He. Therefore it is necessarily obligatory that He, exalted is He, is Knowing of all knowables.

And know that He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾, and did not say: "He knows what is in the earth and what is in the heavens." In observing this order there is a wondrous secret.

Then He, exalted is He, specified what occurs of private conversation among the servants, so He said:

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 58, verses 8–9:

﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

**There are several issues here.**

**The first issue:** Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywa read *"ma takunu min najwa thalathatin"* with a *ta'* (feminine verb form). Then he said: The masculine form that the majority (*al-'amma*) read is the preferable reading, because of the spreading (*al-shiya'*) and generality of the category (*'umum al-jinsiyya*), as in your saying *ma ja'anī min imra'a* ("no woman came to me") and *ma hadara-nī min jariya* ("no slave-girl attended me"). Also, because a separator intervened between the verb and its subject, namely the word *min* ("from"). And because the feminine marking of *najwa* is not genuinely feminine. As for the feminine verb form, it is because the sense of the verse is *ma takunu najwa* ("there will not be a secret conversation"), just as one says *ma qamat imra'atun* ("no woman stood up") and *ma hadarat jariyatun* ("no slave-girl attended").

**The second issue:** His saying *"ma yakun"* uses *kana* in its complete (*al-tammah*) sense, meaning: what does not exist or come into being from a secret conversation of three.

**The third issue:** *Najwa* is the act of conferring in secret, and it is a verbal noun (*masdar*). From it is His saying: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾ (4:114). Al-Zajjaj said: *al-najwa* is derived from *al-najwa*, which means an elevated place that offers safety. So a speech that is kept secret, when it is free from others hearing it, becomes like an elevated ground, for because of its height it is free from others' reach.

It is also permissible to make *al-najwa* a descriptive term, so one says *qawmun najwa* ("a people in secret conference"). His saying ﴿when they are a secret conference﴾ (17:47) means *hum dhawu najwa* ("they are people of secret conference"). The original noun was omitted, and this is the case with every verbal noun that is used as a descriptor.

**The fourth issue:** The genitive case of *thalatha* in His saying ﴿min najwa thalathatin﴾ allows two possibilities:

One: that it is in the genitive by virtue of the construct (*idafa*).

Two: that *najwa* means "those conferring in secret," and the sense is *ma yakunu min mutanajina thalathatan* ("there will not be from those conferring in secret three"), in which case it is a descriptor.

**The fifth issue:** Ibn Abi Abla read *thalathatan* and *khamsatan* in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), with *yatanajawna* implied, because *najwa* indicates it.

**The sixth issue:** He, exalted is He, mentioned three and five and omitted the case of four in between. The scholars gave several reasons for this:

One: This indicates the completeness of mercy. When three people gather, if two of them begin a private conference and consultation, the third remains lonely and isolated, so his heart is constricted, and Allah, exalted is He, says: "I am your companion and your intimate." Likewise with five: when they gather, the fifth remains lonely and solitary. But if they are four, none of them is left alone. This indicates that whoever cuts himself off from the creation, Allah, exalted is He, will not leave him neglected.

Two: The odd number is more noble than the even, because Allah is *witr* (one, odd) and loves the odd. So He specified the odd numbers in mention, as a reminder that the divine affairs must be observed in all matters.

Three: The least that is necessary in a consultation whose purpose is to pave the way for the interest of three is that the two are like disputants over affirmation and negation, and the third is like the intermediary judge between them. Then that consultation is complete and that purpose is achieved. Likewise with every group that gathers for consultation: there must be among them one who is a judge whose word is accepted. For this reason, the people of consultation must be an odd number. So He, glorified is He, mentioned the first two odd numbers and was satisfied with mentioning them as a reminder of the rest.

The third issue: They have mentioned several views in the verse:

The first: the intended meaning is the assembly of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, where they would crowd together out of rivalry for closeness to him and eagerness to hear his speech. On this view they mentioned several reports concerning the occasion of revelation:

The first: Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "On Friday he, peace be upon him, was in the Suffah, and the place was cramped. He would honour the people of Badr among the Muhajirun and the Ansar. Some people from among the people of Badr came, having arrived at the gathering first, and they stood before the Prophet ﷺ, waiting to be given room. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recognised what made them stand, and this grieved the Messenger. He said to those around him who were not of Badr: 'Stand up, so-and-so, then so-and-so.' He continued to seat people in the number of those who were standing before him, and this grieved those who were made to rise from their place, and dislike was seen on their faces. The hypocrites spoke against this, saying: 'By Allah, he has not been just to these people; a group took their places and loved to be near him, so he made them rise and seated those who came late.' So this verse was revealed on Friday."

The second: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: This verse was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn al-Shammas. He entered the mosque when the people had taken their places, and he wished to be near the Messenger, peace be upon him, because of the deafness in his ears. They made room for him until he came near, then some of them crowded him, and words passed between him and them. He described to the Messenger his love of being near him so that he might hear his speech, and that so-and-so had not made room for him. So this verse was revealed, and the people were commanded to make room and that no one should rise for another.

The third: They used to love to be near the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a man among them would dislike being crowded, so his brother might ask him to make room for him and he would refuse. So Allah, Exalted is He, commanded them to show compassion to one another and to bear what is disliked. Among them were some who disliked the poor touching them, and the people of the Suffah wore wool and had odours.

The second view, which is the choice of al-Hasan, is that the intended meaning is making room in the ranks of fighting, like His saying: ﴿seats for fighting﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121]. A man would come to the row and say, "Make room," and they would refuse out of their eagerness for martyrdom.

The third view: the intended meaning is all gatherings and assemblies. Al-Qadi said: The closer view is that the intended meaning is the assembly of the Messenger, peace be upon him, because Allah mentioned "the assembly" in a way that requires it to be known, and what was known at the time of the revelation was only the assembly of the Messenger ﷺ, in which rivalry was great. It is well known that closeness to him had a great merit, because of hearing his words and because of the rank it conferred. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "Let those of mature minds and understanding be nearest to me." For this reason he would place the eminent among his Companions forward, and they, because of their great number, would crowd one another, so they were commanded to make room where possible, for that is more conducive to mutual affection and to sharing in hearing what is necessary in the religion. If this holds in his assembly, then the state of jihad should be similar, nay perhaps more so, since a man of great courage may be behind the first row, and the need for his advance is pressing, so making room is necessary. Then all other assemblies of knowledge and remembrance are judged by analogy to this.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah will make room for you﴾, it is general in respect of everything people seek room in: place, provision, breast (heart), the grave, and Paradise.

A sensible person should not restrict the verse to making room in an assembly; rather, what is meant is conveying good to the Muslim and bringing joy into his heart. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his Muslim brother."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is said, "Rise up," then rise up. God will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees. And God is All-Aware of what you do.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

One: When you are told, "Stand up to make room for the one who enters," then stand up.

Second: When you are told, "Get up from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and do not prolong your talk," then get up and do not linger with him, as He says: ﴿Nor remain, seeking familiarity with conversation. Third: When you are told, "Rise up for the prayer, for jihad, and for acts of good," then busy yourselves with it and prepare for it, and do not be sluggish about it. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: some people were sluggish about the prayer, so they were commanded to stand for it when the call was made.

The second issue: It is recited as "unshuzu" with a kasra and with a damma on the shin, and both are dialectal variants, like ya'kifuna and ya'kufuna, and ya'rishuna and ya'rushuna.

Know that when God, exalted is He, first forbade them from some things, then commanded them to do some things, He promised them rewards for obedience, saying: ﴿God will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees﴾, meaning God raises the believers who comply with the commands of His Messenger, and especially those of them who have knowledge, by degrees. Then, regarding the intended meaning of this elevation, there are two views:

The first, which is a rare view: that it refers to elevation in the assembly of the Messenger, peace be upon him.

The second, which is the well-known view: that it refers to elevation in degrees of reward and ranks of divine pleasure.

Know that we have elaborated in explaining God's words ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31] on the virtue of knowledge. Al-Qadi said: There is no doubt that the knowledge of the learned person brings him a standing in obedience that the believer does not attain. For this reason, the learned person is followed in all his actions, while one who is not learned is not followed, because he knows how to guard against the unlawful and doubtful matters, and how to hold himself accountable, which others do not know; he knows the manner of humility and submissiveness in worship, which others do not know; he knows the manner, times, and qualities of repentance, which others do not know; and he is more careful regarding the rights that are incumbent upon him than others are. There are many other aspects. However, just as the standing of his acts of obedience becomes greater in degree of reward, so too his punishment becomes greater for the sins he commits, because of the position of his knowledge, to the extent that it is not impossible that a minor sin from him be considered a major one, unlike that of others.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 58, verse 12:

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** This obligation includes several kinds of benefit.

The first: it magnifies the Messenger (peace be upon him) and magnifies his private consultation (munajah). When a person obtains something with difficulty, he values it highly, and when he obtains it easily, he holds it cheap.

The second: many of the poor benefit from that charity given before the consultation.
